deepDives.title: Remittances rise 2.7% to $3.55 billion
deepDives.summary: Personal remittances from overseas Filipinos rose by 2.7 percent to $3.55 billion in September, picking up from the previous month and providing continued support to household spending and domestic economic activity.
reasons: reader relevance 3/3: Remittances rose in September, affecting OFW household support

related.title: Cash remittances rose to $3.20B in Sept. 2026 --BSP
related.text:
The country recorded higher cash remittances from overseas Filipino workers in September 2026, posting year-on-year growth, according to data from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) on Monday.
Cash remittances rose to US$3.20 billion in September 2026; this is 2.6% higher than the US$3.12 billion in September 2025.
Month-on-month, money transfers coursed through banks are also up from US $3.035 billion last August.
The United States remains the top source of cash remittances at 39.8%, followed by Singapore at 7.1%, and Saudi Arabia at 6.4%. Money inflows were also logged from Japan at 5.0% and the United Kingdom at 4.7%.
Cash remittances rose to $3.035B in August 2026 — BSP data

BSP maintains 3% a month interest rate cap on credit card transactions
Land-based workers accounted for the bulk of the cash remittances with 80%, while sea-based workers accounted for the remaining 20%.
On the other hand, personal remittances, or the sum of transfers sent in cash or in kind, including those coursed through informal channels, totaled $3.55 billion, up from $3.46 billion in September last year.
"Seasonally adjusted personal remittances also rose moderately in September 2026, indicating sustained underlying growth in remittance inflows after accounting for seasonal factors. Personal remittances include in-kind remittances, aside from cash sent through banks and informal channels," the BSP said.
"Remittance inflows continued to support household consumption and domestic economic activity, underscoring their role as a stable source of household income and foreign exchange for the Philippine economy," it added. —AOL, GMA News

MANILA, Philippines — Personal remittances from overseas Filipinos rose by 2.7 percent to $3.55 billion in September, picking up from the previous month and providing continued support to household spending and domestic economic activity.
Data from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) showed the broader measure of remittances increased from $3.46 billion in September 2025 and $3.37 billion in August. Personal remittances include cash sent through banks and informal channels as well as transfers in kind.
Meanwhile, cash remittances, which cover money sent by land-based and sea-based workers through the banking system, increased by 2.6 percent to $3.2 billion from $3.12 billion a year earlier. The September level was also higher than the $3.04 billion recorded in August.
For the nine-month period ending September, personal remittances grew by 2.3 percent to $29.65 billion from $28.97 billion in the same period last year. Cash remittances likewise expanded by 2.3 percent to $26.63 billion from $26.03 billion.
Remittances remain an important source of income for Filipino households, supporting spending on everyday needs while providing the economy with a stable stream of foreign exchange.
Personal remittances were equivalent to 8.4 percent of gross domestic product as of the third quarter, while cash remittances accounted for 7.5 percent.
The United States remained the largest reported source of cash remittances, followed by Singapore and Saudi Arabia.
John Paolo Rivera, senior research fellow at the Philippine Institute for Development Studies, said inflows could strengthen toward the Christmas season as overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) typically send additional funds home for holiday spending and other household needs.
However, stronger inflows would not necessarily translate into faster year-on-year growth because of base effects, or comparisons against already elevated levels a year ago, as well as uncertainties in labor markets overseas.
“Remittances should remain an important source of support for household consumption and economic activity during the fourth quarter,” Rivera said.
Jonathan Ravelas, senior adviser at Reyes, Tacandong & Co., likewise expects remittances to receive a seasonal boost toward year-end as OFWs send more money home for Christmas-related expenses.
“The holiday season should provide a lift to remittances in the coming months as OFWs traditionally send more money to support year-end spending,” Ravelas said.
“While growth may improve from September, the pace will still depend on global economic conditions and developments in key OFW markets, particularly the Middle East,” he said.
Ravelas added that remittances would remain an important pillar of household consumption and overall economic growth.

related.title: Fuel prices to go down anew on November 17
related.text:
Motorists will enjoy another round of fuel price cuts starting Tuesday, November 17, as oil companies announced another rollback in pump prices.
In an advisory, the Department of Energy (DOE) said gasoline prices will go down by P1.50 per liter across all grades.
Diesel prices, including Diesel Plus, will drop by P3.80 per liter, while kerosene prices will decrease by P5.80 per liter.
"These changes are based on movements in the global oil market, amid ongoing developments in the Middle East affecting global supply and prices," the DOE said.

The Department of Energy (DOE) announced the following price adjustments on Monday, Nov. 16:
The new prices are expected to remain in effect through Monday, Nov. 23.
The latest reductions follow last week's steep P16.80-per-liter cut in gasoline prices, along with rollbacks of P4.10 for diesel and P3.70 for kerosene.
The DOE said the price reductions must be implemented in full.
Industry forecasts late last week had pointed to larger cuts for gasoline. The DOE's announced adjustments, however, come as the country remains under a state of national energy emergency.

The decline has come despite the weakening Philippine peso, which closed at P63.72 against the US dollar on Friday, November 13, near the P64 level.
A weaker peso makes dollar-denominated fuel imports more expensive, potentially offsetting some of the relief from lower international oil prices.

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court (SC) has rendered unconstitutional a bond requirement for seafarers seeking to execute monetary awards and damages under Republic Act 12021 or the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers.
Under Section 59 of the said law, seafarers seeking to execute monetary awards and damages should post a bond “to ensure restitution should the award be subsequently reversed or modified.”
However, the SC said the bond requirement “violated the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Constitution (as it) imposed a financial burden on seafarers seeking to enforce favorable labor judgments and subjected them to a disadvantage not similarly imposed on other workers.”
It also voided related orders from the Department of Labor and Employment that enforced the bond requirement, and from the Department of Migrant Workers on the use of its Agarang Kalinga at Saklolo Para sa mga OFW na Nangangailangan fund to pay bond premiums.
At the same time, Section 1, Rule XXII of the implementing rules and regulations of RA 12021 was “declared ultra vires and void” for “contravening” another provision in the law that “preserves the rights, privileges and benefits previously enjoyed by Filipino seafarers before its effectivity.”
Also declared unconstitutional was Section 60 of the same law and Section 4 of RA 10706 or the Seafarers Protection Act, which both imposed rules on how lawyers should represent seafarers in related cases, including “a 10 percent ceiling on fees, requirements for notarized certifications and undertakings and rules governing the collection of fees from seafarers.”
“While Congress may enact measures to protect seafarers against ambulance chasing and abusive practices, the regulation of lawyers’ professional conduct and the practice of law remains within the Supreme Court’s exclusive authority,” it maintained.
On the other hand, the high court upheld the constitutionality of other provisions in the Magna Carta on maritime education and training. It declared that under the said law, the Maritime Industry Authority was authorized to impose “standards intended to ensure the quality of maritime education, the competency of Filipino seafarers and compliance with applicable international maritime standards.”
“Particularly, the requirements relating to enrollment and available shipboard training opportunities were considered reasonable measures to address the availability of practical training for maritime students. The prohibition against charging tuition or matriculation fees for shipboard training conducted by third-party providers was likewise sustained as a measure against unjustified charges,” the SC noted.
The decision penned by SC Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh resolved the five consolidated petitions raised by seafarers, labor organizations and maritime educational institutions against the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers.

MANILA, Philippines — Filipino seafarers who win monetary awards in labor disputes will no longer be required to post a bond to collect disputed amounts while their cases are under appeal.
Earlier this month, the Supreme Court struck down a key provision of the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers.
The high court ruled that the requirement placed an unfair financial burden on seafarers seeking to enforce favorable labor judgments. The demand, the court argued, puts them at a disadvantage compared with other workers who face no similar restriction.
In a decision penned by Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh during its November 11 session, the Supreme Court partially granted five consolidated petitions challenging provisions of Republic Act 12021, or the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers, and its implementing rules.
The ruling, announced Monday, November 16, also invalidated provisions restricting lawyers' fees and legal representation of seafarers. It upheld separate regulations governing maritime education and training.
Under Section 59 of the 2024 law, monetary awards covering wages, statutory benefits and undisputed amounts were immediately enforceable.
But seafarers seeking to collect disputed amounts and damages while an appeal or judicial review was pending had to post a bond guaranteeing repayment if the award was later reversed or modified.
The Supreme Court declared the requirement unconstitutional for violating the due process and equal protection clauses of the Constitution.
The justices acknowledged the government's interest in preventing "ambulance chasing," or the improper solicitation of legal clients, and protecting the maritime industry against monetary awards that could not be recovered if overturned.
They ruled, however, that these objectives did not justify imposing the additional financial burden on seafarers.
The court also struck down a provision allowing the Department of Migrant Workers' AKSYON Fund to pay bond premiums, finding that the arrangement failed to meet the constitutional requirement that public funds be used for a public purpose.
Consequently, Sections 4 and 5, Rule III of Department of Labor and Employment Department Order No. 247, which implemented the bond requirement, were also declared unconstitutional and void.
The court further invalidated Section 1, Rule XXII of the law's implementing rules insofar as it applied the bond requirement to monetary awards arising from complaints filed on or after the law took effect.
It found that the provision exceeded the authority granted by the law and contradicted Section 94, which preserves rights, privileges and benefits previously enjoyed by Filipino seafarers.
Restrictions on lawyers' fees invalidated
The Supreme Court similarly struck down Section 60 of RA 12021 and Section 4 of RA 10706, or the Seafarers Protection Act, saying they regulate the practice of law.
The provisions imposed restrictions on legal representation, including a 10% ceiling on lawyers' fees, mandatory notarized certifications and undertakings, and rules governing the collection of fees from seafarers.
While Congress may legislate against abusive legal practices, regulating lawyers' professional conduct falls under the judiciary's exclusive constitutional authority, the court ruled.
The Federation of Free Workers, one of the petitioners, welcomed the ruling as a victory for seafarers pursuing labor claims.
"Sa wakas, may pasya na! Dalawang isyu ang inilapit namin sa Korte Suprema, at sa pareho ay nanaig ang mga marino. Tagumpay ito ng mga manggagawa, lalo na ng marinong umuwing may pinsala at ng pamilyang naghihintay ng pambili ng gamot," the federation's national president Sonny Matula said.
("Finally, there is a decision! We brought two issues before the Supreme Court, and the seafarers prevailed in both. This is a victory for workers, especially for the seafarer who came home injured and the family waiting for money to buy medicine.")
Maritime education rules upheld
The Supreme Court, however, rejected challenges by the Philippine Association of Maritime Institutions Inc. and other maritime schools against Sections 75, 76 and 78 of the law.
The schools had questioned provisions transferring regulatory authority over maritime education to the Maritime Industry Authority, linking enrollment to available shipboard training slots and prohibiting tuition or matriculation fees for shipboard training conducted by third-party providers.
The justices ruled that these requirements did not violate academic freedom, describing them as reasonable government regulations intended to maintain educational standards, ensure student competency and comply with international maritime requirements.
The court also upheld the procedure by which Congress enacted the Magna Carta, finding compliance with constitutional requirements, including the three-reading rule, presentment requirements and the one-title-one-subject rule.
It likewise sustained the president's certification of urgency and the actions of the bicameral conference committee.
The Supreme Court emphasized that the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers remains valid and enforceable, except for the provisions expressly declared unconstitutional or void.

MANILA, Philippines — Around 600,000 overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) across Southeast Asia stand to benefit from the adoption by ASEAN leaders of the Philippine-spearheaded “ASEAN Declaration on Fair, Ethical and Sustainable Recruitment for Empowered Migrant Workers.”
In a statement, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) said the declaration would establish region-wide standards to curb excessive recruitment fees, dismantle cyberscam trafficking networks and strengthen cross-border legal protections for millions of Southeast Asian workers.
“This Declaration advances ASEAN instruments toward the protection and promotion of rights of migrant workers. With this Declaration, there will be greater transparency and accountability in recruitment and placement across all ASEAN member-states – prohibiting excessive or unreasonable recruitment fees, strengthening agency licensing and monitoring and promoting access to justice and complaint mechanisms,” DMW Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac said.
Cacdac said the pact directly strengthens cross-border cooperation to dismantle cyber-scam hubs – an urgent operational priority, as the DMW and the Philippine embassy in Yangon actively monitor approximately 90 to 100 Filipinos allegedly trapped in Myanmar-based scam compounds.

ASEAN member states backed the full implementation of the ASEAN Petroleum Security Agreement during meetings Sunday, November 15, Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said.

opinions.summary: First it was the Marcos Cabinet that went after PhilHealth funds, falsely claiming a so-called “surplus” or excess unused funds that were from government contributions. In a matter of weeks if not days, the funds were transferred to Alibaba’s cave at the DOF.

First it was the Marcos Cabinet that went after PhilHealth funds, falsely claiming a so-called “surplus” or excess unused funds that were from government contributions. In a matter of weeks if not days, the funds were transferred to Alibaba’s cave at the DOF.
Thanks to the Supreme Court, the justices nullified the claim of the DOF and the Marcos government and ordered them to return the funds, which were members’ contributions and not a government grant.
So far I have not heard of any of those officials going to jail nor have the funds been fully returned or restored. God willing the day will come when they face charges and pay the price for such a vile misrepresentation.

The last time ASEAN leaders gathered in Manila, in 2017, Angkas was barely a year on the road. We had no legal framework, a few thousand riders and a business many people told me was not a real business at all. I sat in the summit traffic like everyone else and asked the question many of you are asking this week. What does any of this have to do with me?
Nine years later I have my answer. Almost everything.
Start with what ASEAN is, minus the big words. It is a neighborhood association of 11 countries and about 680 million people. When the neighbors agree on common rules, a small shop in Marikina can sell to a customer in Jakarta almost as easily as to one in Makati.
